structure.title: Essays 1–14 · Would division make anybody safer?
structure.text: The writers ask their New York readers to imagine several American confederacies instead of one Union. Rival trade interests, border quarrels and foreign alliances give that imagined map consequences far beyond the administrative convenience of drawing smaller districts.

structure.title: Essays 15–36 · Give public decisions the means to work
structure.text: Under the existing Confederation common decisions could depend on member states supplying money or compliance. Taxation, defence and enforcement become tests of whether an obligation imposed on a government can survive its lack of direct means.

structure.title: Essays 37–51 · How can power be made to check power?
structure.text: The proposed Constitution must now be defended against fears about the power just claimed for it. Lines drawn on paper require institutions with motives and resources to defend those lines when an officeholder tries to cross them.

structure.title: Essays 52–85 · Inspect the offices one by one
structure.text: Representation, elections, the Senate, the executive and the courts receive separate defences. By the end, small matters such as term length or who proposes an appointment have carried a surprising amount of the argument about liberty.

people.name: Publius
people.text: Hamilton, Madison and Jay write under a common name for readers deciding on ratification. The signature gives eighty-five occasional essays a public speaker, though the emphasis and immediate opponent can change as the series proceeds.

people.name: Faction
people.role: A group capable of sacrificing other people's rights
people.text: The problem becomes especially hard when the faction is itself a majority. A system of voting can register its strength perfectly well while leaving unanswered what will protect the people it means to injure.

people.name: The energetic executive
people.role: A proposed advantage that sounds like a danger
people.text: Hamilton argues that placing executive responsibility in one identifiable officer can make blame easier to assign. The same feature an opponent fears as monarchical is offered as a condition for accountability.

context.title: Read as a case for ratification
context.text: These essays aim to persuade before the proposed institutions have operated. Their predictions about what officeholders will want are crucial evidence of the design's intended logic and remain predictions open to challenge.

notice.text: Compare the two uses of scale.
notice.why: A large republic might seem too big for self-government. Madison asks whether its greater number of interests might make an oppressive coalition harder to assemble, turning a familiar objection into a proposed safeguard.

notice.text: Watch qualifications slip into a confident forecast.
notice.why: A mechanism works if voters can identify responsibility, officials defend their offices or ambitions compete as predicted. Each condition marks a place where the defence can be tested independently of the desirability of the goal.

opening: The revolution has succeeded, and the new American union may still fail. Hamilton, Madison, and Jay must persuade readers to accept a stronger government without dismissing the fear that strong governments abuse their power. Their essays work through representation, faction, courts, and rival institutions, treating ambition as something a constitution must expect. The interest lies in watching political ideals become machinery: rules intended to keep people with competing interests governing together even when virtue is in short supply and nobody wants to lose.
